angle: question hook: can you measure the whole Earth with a stick; rule out walking around it or going to space: you need noon; Syene: noon sun straight down a well, no shadow; same noon in Alexandria a stick's shadow is 7.2 degrees; parallel rays -> same angle at the Earth's centre; re-hook: 7.2 is one fiftieth of a circle, so Earth = 50 slices; pace it: 5,000 stadia x 50 = 250,000; short stadion -> 40,000 km vs real 40,008 (stadion length disputed); DIY: friend 1,000 km south -> 9 degrees; checkable CTA (500 km -> 4.5 degrees)
title: How to measure the whole Earth with a stick
description:
At noon on the longest day the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene (Aswan), while a stick in Alexandria, further north, cast a shadow of 7.2 degrees. Sunlight arrives in parallel rays, so that angle is also the slice of the Earth between the two cities: one fiftieth of a circle. The cities were 5,000 stadia apart, so the Earth is 50 x 5,000 = 250,000 stadia around. How long a stadion was is still argued (about 160 to 210 m); the short one gives 40,000 km, against a real 40,008 km around the poles. Eratosthenes, about 240 BC.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py). Source: Wikipedia, Eratosthenes (method as told by Cleomedes) and Earth's circumference.
social_caption: One stick, one shadow and one long walk were enough to measure the whole Earth, 2,200 years ago. Here's how you'd do it yourself.
facts_checked: Method (Cleomedes' account): noon on the summer solstice, Sun straight down a well in Syene, a gnomon in Alexandria casts a shadow of 7.2 degrees = 1/50 of a circle; 5,000 stadia apart; 250,000 stadia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eratosthenes)
Parallel sunlight: the shadow angle equals the angle at Earth's centre between the cities (alternate angles; Wikipedia, Eratosthenes)
Stadion length uncertain, about 160 to 210 m (Wikipedia, Eratosthenes); 250,000 x 160 m = 40,000 km (verify.py)
Real polar (meridional) circumference about 40,008 km; equatorial 40,075 km (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_circumference)
DIY: 1,000 km north-south -> 1000/40008 x 360 = 9.0 degrees; CTA 500 km -> 4.5 degrees (verify.py)

beats.say: Can you measure the whole Earth with a stick?
You don't walk around it, and you don't need space. You need noon.
Find a town where the noon sun shines straight down a well. In Syene, on the longest day, there's no shadow at all.
Same day, same noon, stand a stick up in Alexandria, far to the north. It casts a shadow: 7.2 degrees.
Sunlight arrives in parallel lines. So that angle is also the slice of Earth between the two towns.
And 7.2 degrees is one fiftieth of a circle. The whole Earth is just 50 of those slices.
Pay a surveyor to pace the distance: 5,000 stadia. Times 50 is 250,000.
Historians still argue how long a stadion was. The short one gives 40,000 kilometers. The real answer: 40,008.
Try it yourself. With a friend 1,000 kilometers south, your noon shadows differ by about 9 degrees.
So if your friend's 500 kilometers away, how far apart are your shadows?
